findings.title: A throttled judge session loops forever inside a gate, and the theory cannot finish while it does
findings.claim: §5.4 step 3 runs the judge through the same `_run_agent` as the interpretation session ("The judge's nested `_run_agent` keeps its own recycle budget"), and §15.5's `_judge` catches only `except Exception`. But `_run_agent`'s throttle arms never raise and never consume the budget: `except ReachLimitError: await asyncio.sleep(1200); return await _run_agent(make_driver, depth)` and `except RateLimitError: await asyncio.sleep(2); return await _run_agent(make_driver, depth)` (semantic_interpretation.py:818-827) re-enter with `depth` UNCHANGED. So a judge that meets a usage cap or a 429 retries without bound; the exception never reaches `_judge`, so D10's "an outcome the gate could not judge is CHANGED" is never reached for the two failure modes that are by far the most likely. Because §5.3's termination rule keeps the loop alive until `gates_running == 0` and `interpret_file` returns only after the gate task group has joined, one throttled judge pins the whole theory: the interpretation session stays open, the ML worker thread stays blocked in `dispatch_loop`, and (after §8) the interpretation lock stays held. Worse, a usage cap is account-wide, so it hits every gate and the interpretation session at once: N judges each wake after 20 min and re-fire simultaneously, and the 2 s rate-limit arm gives a fixed, non-growing retry interval, i.e. a self-sustaining 429 storm rather than a backoff.
findings.evidence: semantic_interpretation.py:818-827 (`return await _run_agent(make_driver, depth)` in both throttle arms — depth not incremented, unlike the two recycle arms at :841 and :862); §15.5 `_judge` catches `except Exception`, which `_run_agent` never lets a throttle escape as; §5.3 pseudo-loop line "await every gate -- the gate task group (§5.4), before the session is closed"; §15.4 `if not task.gates_running: break`.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the throttle arms budget-aware on the task rather than global: give `AgentTask` a `throttle_budget` (interpretation task: unbounded, today's behaviour; `JudgeTask`: e.g. one 2 s rate-limit retry and zero usage-cap waits) that `_run_agent` reads before sleeping, and let it re-raise `ReachLimitError`/`RateLimitError` past the budget. `_judge` then catches them like any other failure and resolves CHANGED (D10, conservative and free), instead of the run hanging on a decision whose default answer is already known.

findings.title: The gate TaskGroup turns every interpret_file failure into an ExceptionGroup, losing FatalAgentError and the user-error marker path
findings.plan_sections: §5.4 "Failures (D10)" ("it fails the task group and therefore `interpret_file`"); §15.1 (`GateError`); §15.4; §10 ("`GateError` fails the run", "`CancelledError` propagates")
findings.claim: The plan puts `_run_agent` inside an `asyncio.TaskGroup` owned by `interpret_file` and reasons about failures as if the raised exception reached the caller unchanged. It does not: CPython's TaskGroup wraps EVERY exception that escapes the body or a child in a `BaseExceptionGroup` (verified on this machine's Python 3.12.3: a single `ValueError` in a child comes out as `ExceptionGroup`). Three consequences the plan does not account for. (a) `FatalAgentError` no longer arrives as `FatalAgentError`: the ML side's one-line user error depends on `extract_user_error` finding `USER_ERROR_MARKER` and returning EVERYTHING after it (semantic_store.ML:1435-1445), so the user now also gets the exception-group frame junk that follows the message, and with two sub-exceptions (a `GateError` plus the loop's own error) the first marker wins arbitrarily. (b) Any `except FatalAgentError` stops matching — the existing suite already asserts the bare class through `interpret_file` (archive/tests/test_interpretation_driver.py:293), and §10's "`GateError` fails the run" test would have to be written against `ExceptionGroup`, which is a test written around a defect rather than against a contract. (c) The 3 s cancel path of rpc.py:349-360 delivers `CancelledError` into the group, whose `__aexit__` re-raises it uncombined only when nothing else failed — a gate that fails *while* being cancelled produces a mixed group.
findings.evidence: asyncio/taskgroups.py `TaskGroup.__aexit__` raises `BaseExceptionGroup(...)`; semantic_store.ML:1435-1445 `extract_user_error`/`interpretation_rpc_error`; archive/tests/test_interpretation_driver.py:230,293 (`pytest.raises(FatalAgentError)`); semantic_interpretation.py:718-723 (`USER_ERROR_MARKER` contract).
findings.proposed_fix: Unwrap at the one place that owns the group, so the failure contract of `interpret_file` is unchanged: `try: async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: ... except BaseExceptionGroup as eg:` re-raise the first non-`CancelledError` leaf (flattened) `from eg`, and re-raise `CancelledError` as itself. State this in §5.4 next to "fails the task group and therefore `interpret_file`", and write §10's tests against the unwrapped class.

findings.title: Unlimited concurrent judge sessions means hundreds of agent CLI subprocesses at once (spec relaxation of D12)
findings.plan_sections: §5.4 ("one asyncio task per entity in an `asyncio.TaskGroup`, no concurrency limit"); D12; §5.3.1 "Cost"; §15.3 `start_gate`
findings.claim: SPEC RELAXATION of D12's "there is no limit on how many judge sessions run at once". The concurrency is not a handful: the `answer` tool takes an ARRAY, so one tool call routinely answers a whole batch and `on_answer` starts up to `_BATCH_SIZE = 20` gates in one handler invocation (semantic_interpretation.py:130, :577-620); the plan itself notes independent theories run concurrently under `schedule_dag`, and those are separate `interpret_file` coroutines on ONE event loop in ONE host process (schedule_dag forks one Future per theory, semantic_store.ML:1986-1993, each taking its own pooled RPC connection). With Isabelle's default worker count that is easily 8-32 theories × up to 20 judges = 160-640 fresh agent sessions live at once, each a Claude Code / Codex CLI subprocess with its own ~55k-token context (D3) and, on the Codex path, its own registered MCP HTTP session (mcp_server.py:254-262). That is a memory and file-descriptor blow-up, and it is also the direct cause of the 429 storm in concurrency-1. The gain from unbounded concurrency is bounded: a judge takes 8-20 s (D3) while a batch turn takes minutes, so a modest cap costs almost no wall-clock.
findings.evidence: semantic_interpretation.py:130 (`_BATCH_SIZE = 20`), :577-651 (`_answer_tool` loops over `args["interpretations"]`, i.e. many entries per call); semantic_store.ML:1978-1993 (one Future per theory under a shared group, all calling the same host); interpretation_driver/mcp_server.py:254-262 (`register_session` per driver instance); claude_code.py:461-484 (`ClaudeSDKClient.__aenter__` spawns the CLI per driver).
findings.proposed_fix: Keep D12's semantics (one entity per judge session, a fresh session each time, the gate started the moment the answer arrives) and bound only how many judge SESSIONS run simultaneously: a module-level `asyncio.Semaphore(_MAX_CONCURRENT_JUDGES)` (process-wide, so it also covers concurrent theories) acquired around step 3 of `_gate` only. Steps 2, 4, 5 and 6 stay unthrottled, no verdict changes, and the queue's termination logic is untouched because a gate waiting on the semaphore is still counted in `gates_running`.

findings.title: The prefilter's vector store is smuggled through process-global server state, stale across runs and bound to a pooled connection
findings.plan_sections: §15.8 "Ordering of the startup check's result"; §5.6; §5.4 step 2; D5
findings.claim: §15.8 has the startup-check RPC park the resolved `Semantic_Vector_Store` on `connection.server.gate_emb_store` and every theory's `interpret_file` read it back. `server` is the process's single `Server` object (rpc.py:242-263, one per host, shared by every connection), so this is process-global mutable state with a per-run meaning, and the plan gives it no reset: "a missing attribute means 'not checked'" only covers the FIRST run. A second cone run whose startup check fails therefore inherits run 1's store and silently prefilters with a stale endpoint/model — which directly contradicts D5 ("the prefilter embedding model follows `Semantic_Embedding.embedding_model`"), since that option is read per run from the user's `cfg_context`. Second problem: the store is constructed as `Semantic_Vector_Store(emb_provider=provider, connection=self)` (semantics.py:2811) bound to the connection the startup check ran on — and `call_command` hands that connection straight back to the pool (RPC.ML:883-894), from where a failed heartbeat closes it along with every other pooled connection (RPC.ML:867-878). The long-lived global then holds a closed/foreign connection, which is a latent hazard for anything on the store beyond `.emb_provider`.
findings.evidence: rpc.py:242-263 (one `Server` per process; `Connection.server` is that object); semantics.py:2792-2811 (`_conn_semantic_vector_store`, `connection=self`); RPC.ML:867-895 (`get_connection` closes the whole pool on a failed heartbeat; `call_command` releases the connection back to the pool); §5.6 (`_resolve_embedding_config` is per-run, over `cfg_context`).
findings.proposed_fix: Drop `server.gate_emb_store`. §5.6 already adds `Config.make_config_lookup_callback` to `send_for_interpretation`'s callback list, so `interpret_file` can resolve its own store on ITS OWN connection: `try: emb_store = await connection.semantic_vector_store() except Exception: emb_store = None` (the same call the plan already names, semantics.py:2792). That is per-run and per-context by construction — D5 holds with nothing to remember — and the startup check keeps exactly one job: printing text §12 #4 once. If the once-per-run report must gate the theories, pass a boolean, not an object.

findings.title: The interpretation lock is released by the peer noticing EOF, so ML's return does not mean the lock is free
findings.plan_sections: §8.1 ("Owned by the RPC connection that acquired it ... No release procedure, no sidecar"); §8.2; D8
findings.claim: §8.2's `with_interpretation_lock` ends by closing the lock connection, and §8.1 makes the release a side effect of `Connection.close()` on the Python side. But closing a socket in ML is not synchronised with the peer's reaction: the release happens only after the host's event loop schedules the reader task's EOF, `read()` raises, `handle_client` unwinds to its `finally` and calls `close()` (rpc.py:117-123, :374-377). The ML command returns immediately, before any of that. So a run that has visibly finished can still hold the lock, and because D8 is try-once-never-wait, the very next `run_semantic_interpretation` fails hard with text §12 #2 for no real reason. The window is not always sub-millisecond: this host's loop is regularly blocked in synchronous work (whole-store SIMD `topk` scans, LMDB write transactions), and back-to-back runs are a normal shape — a script, the `collect` CLI, or two `by aoa` startup checks in consecutive commands. §8.1 analyses only the opposite direction (a cancelled handler still writing after a new run acquires); this direction is not mentioned.
findings.evidence: rpc.py:117-123 (reader task turns EOF into the `read()` sentinel), :374-377 (`finally: ... connection.close()` — the only place the lock could be released), :226-233 (`close()` just closes the writer); RPC.ML:334-338 (`close_connection` returns as soon as the ML streams are closed); plan §12 #2 (lock-busy is an `error`, not a wait).
findings.proposed_fix: Make the release synchronous with respect to ML and keep `on_close` as the crash backstop: add `Semantic_Store.release_interpretation_lock` (releases and clears the FileLock on the connection, idempotent), and have `with_interpretation_lock`'s finaliser call it and AWAIT the reply before `close_connection`. The connection can then also go back to the pool via `release_connection` instead of being thrown away. `on_close` stays registered, so a killed ML process still frees the lock — the invariant is unchanged, the race is gone.

findings.title: A dead embedding service stalls every in-flight gate for ~17 minutes before the prefilter is disabled
findings.plan_sections: §5.4 step 2 ("skipped ... for the rest of the run after a failed call"); §15.5 `_prefilter`; §12 #5
findings.claim: §5.4 step 2 and §15.5 read as though a failed embedding call returns quickly and flips `task.prefilter_disabled`. It does not: `Embedding_Provider.embed` goes through `_embed_cached`, which retries each chunk TEN times with `await asyncio.sleep(2 ** attempt)` — 1+2+...+512 s ≈ 17 minutes — before raising (semantic_embedding.py:351-372). The plan's own §5.6 comment already knows this shape ("failing NOW beats failing after ~17 minutes of 401 retries", semantics.py:2765-2767). Because gates are unlimited and concurrent, every gate already in flight when the endpoint dies pays the full 17 minutes independently — the flag is only set by the first one to give up — and `interpret_file` cannot return until they all join (§5.3 termination). Each attempt also calls `_warn` (semantic_embedding.py:440-452), i.e. one Isabelle warning per attempt per gate: with 20 gates that is 200 warnings for one outage. The startup check (§5.6) does not cover this: it only resolves configuration and constructs the provider; the plan states network reachability is first known here.
findings.evidence: semantic_embedding.py:351-372 (`for attempt in range(10): ... await asyncio.sleep(2 ** attempt)`), :440-452 (`_warn` per failed attempt), :456-468 (`embed` → `_embed_cached`); semantics.py:2765-2767 (the same 17-minute figure, cited as a reason to fail early); plan §5.3 "Termination".
findings.proposed_fix: The prefilter is an optional optimisation whose failure answer is already defined (skip it and let the judge decide), so it must not inherit the corpus-embedding retry policy. Either wrap the call in `async with asyncio.timeout(_PREFILTER_TIMEOUT)` (a few seconds) inside `_prefilter`, or give `Embedding_Provider` an explicit `attempts` parameter (default 10, prefilter 1) threaded to `_embed_cached`'s loop — the latter is the reuse-friendly shape. Set `task.prefilter_disabled = True` on the first failure and have gates re-check it after every await, so gates already waiting bail out instead of each serving their own 17-minute sentence.

findings.title: D14 inverts "answered means durable", but the completeness invariant still tests `results`, so a gate that never starts loses an entity silently
findings.claim: Today `task.results[key] is not None` means the record is on disk: `_answer_tool` deliberately persists first and marks second, and the comment at semantic_interpretation.py:602-614 records that marking first is exactly what once let an entry be dropped for a whole run "silently, because the MCP SDK turns a handler exception into an isError result for the agent and nothing reaches Isabelle". §15.3's `on_answer` reverses that order — `self.results[key] = text` (memory only, D14), then `self.state[idx] = _GATING`, then `self.start_gate(idx)` — so the durability meaning is gone while the check that relies on it is kept verbatim ("today's retry loop, `batch_remaining` and the completeness invariant are unchanged", §5.3.1; the check is semantic_interpretation.py:1225,1241). The gap is reachable: `start_gate` calls `TaskGroup.create_task`, which raises `RuntimeError` when the group is `_aborting` or `_exiting` (asyncio/taskgroups.py) — e.g. another gate has just raised `GateError`, or the loop broke while a late correction turn was still running. The tool handler swallows that into the agent's `errors` list, and the entry is left marked answered, in state `_GATING`, with nothing written and no one waiting for it. The same call order also leaks `gates_running` (incremented before `create_task`, decremented only by `_gate`'s `finally`), which would hang the loop's termination test if the group were not aborting anyway.
findings.evidence: semantic_interpretation.py:602-620 ("PERSIST FIRST, MARK IN MEMORY SECOND" and the per-item `except Exception` that turns a failure into an `errors` entry), :1225 and :1241 (the completeness check counts non-None `results`); semantic_store.ML:2010-2013 (`interpret_cone` calls `mark_interpreted thy` as soon as `interpret'` returns); asyncio/taskgroups.py `create_task` (`RuntimeError` when `_exiting`/`_aborting`).
findings.proposed_fix: Make the state, not the text, the certificate — the shape then cannot be violated by forgetting: (1) in `on_answer`, create the gate task FIRST and only assign `state[idx] = _GATING`, bump `gates_running` and store `results[key]` after `create_task` returns, so a refused task leaves the entry cleanly unanswered and re-askable; (2) change `interpret_file`'s final invariant from "every `results` non-None" to "every enrolled entry is `_DONE`" (non-enrolled entries were filled from the store and were never this run's business). Say so in §5.3.1 where it claims the invariant is unchanged: under D14 it is unchanged in form only.

findings.title: §15.5's `_write` overwrites the persistent row's `None` snapshot and dereferences a `None` record
findings.claim: The `_write` blueprint is not implementable as written, in two ways that both end inside the `gate_write` transaction and therefore, per §5.4, as a `GateError` that kills the run or as a silently wrong record. (a) `ia` is computed in the untracked branch (`ia = eff_star(task, e) if e.deps else None`) and then UNCONDITIONALLY reassigned four lines later (`ia = eff_star(task, e)  # after this entity's own mint`), outside any branch. A persistent-theory entry therefore gets a non-None `interpreted_at`, contradicting §3's last row ("None (all gate fields None)"), D15 ("persistent carry `None` everywhere") and §9 ("What does NOT change: persistent theories"). (b) `version = (rec.version or w.counter_value()) if e.deps else None` dereferences `rec`, which §15.5 itself binds as `rec = task.recs[idx]` — the record BEFORE this run — and which is `None` for every uncached entry; a first-written theorem-alike entity therefore raises `AttributeError` inside the transaction. Today's equivalent guards for exactly this (`rec.version if rec is not None and rec.version else epsilon`, semantic_interpretation.py:944-948).
findings.evidence: plan §15.5 `_write` code block (the second `ia = eff_star(task, e)` is at the same indentation as the `if/elif` chain, not inside it; `rec.version` in the `not tracked` branch); §3 table rows 4-5; semantic_interpretation.py:941-952 (today's None-safe version selection for both untracked and never-digested records).
findings.proposed_fix: Compute `ia` in exactly one place, guarded by the same predicate as `version`: `ia = eff_star(task, e) if (tracked or e.deps) else None`, placed after the `rec_cache` provisional write and with no second assignment; and write the theorem-alike version as `(rec.version if rec is not None and rec.version else w.counter_value())`, reusing today's wording. Better still, since three of the five rows differ only in (version, baseline, digest, deps), have the branch produce that 4-tuple and let one tail compute `ia` and call `put_interpretation` — then the persistent row's `None` cannot be overwritten by a later line.

accurate: The core control-flow design of the run is sound and I found no lost wake-up, no deadlock in the queue loop, and no torn write. `wait_for_progress` is correct as specified: `await _progress.wait()` followed by `clear()` with no await between the clear and the subsequent `next_batch()`/`gates_running` reads means a set that happens after the clear is retained and one that happens before it is observed in the state the loop then reads — the loop genuinely cannot exit with an enrolment unsent, and a gate finishing during a long `run_turn` costs at most one harmless spurious wake. The decision to count `gates_running` synchronously in the answer tool (rather than deriving it from task liveness) is what makes the termination test race-free, and keeping the gates in a group owned by `interpret_file` rather than in the driver session is right: a recycle of the interpretation session provably cannot disturb a running gate, and §5.3.1's four-way state dispatch closes the enrolment window in both directions (a mint before the dependent's write is picked up by that write's own `eff*`; a mint after it is picked up by the snapshot raise). The storage side is likewise safe under concurrency for the reason §15.5 gives: `gate_write` contains no `await`, so on a single event loop no two gates can interleave inside a transaction, `rec_cache` write-back is atomic with respect to other gates, and `invalidate_vectors` touches only the `vector_*` environments (semantic_embedding.py:1126-1180), so `put_interpretation`'s vector-first ordering cannot self-deadlock the semantics environment. The cancellation story holds: `_gate` re-raising `CancelledError` explicitly, the mint living in the same transaction as the record that stores it, and `_propagate`'s separate transactions all failing in the safe direction (a low snapshot is re-listed next scan) means no cancellation path can leave a mint without its record. `write_cost` from many concurrent tasks onto one theory-status key is also correct as-is, since each read-modify-write is one synchronous transaction over its own `total_*` delta. Finally, §8.2's ML lock idiom is right in the detail that matters most — the finaliser is armed before the connection exists, and `Thread_Attributes.uninterruptible`'s signature (thread_attributes.ML:20) does accept the `fn run =>` form the plan uses, keeping `get_connection ()` interruptible inside the bubble.

findings.title: §3 row 1 raises an existing record's version to ε without a mint, so its dependents go stale with nothing enrolling them
findings.claim: §3 row 1 fires when `R is absent OR R.semantic_digest is None`, and prescribes `version := ε` in both cases; §15.5 implements it as `elif verdict is None: version, baseline = w.counter_value(), text`, with no mint and (correctly, for row 1) no propagation. For a record that already carries a version — the never-digested legacy record of parent §4.4 — ε (the counter value at write time) is >= that stored version and usually strictly greater, so the entity's version RISES without a mint. §5.3.1's and §14's soundness argument is explicitly "every stale entity is either a seed or enrolled by the mint that made it stale"; a version raise that is not a mint enrols nobody, so the run ends with theory-internal dependents stale, and `interpret_cone` marks the theory anyway. Today's scan does not do this: it preserves the stored version.
findings.evidence: Plan line 78 `-> version := ε (counter value at write, parent §4.4)`; plan line 926-927 `elif verdict is None: version, baseline = w.counter_value(), text`; plan line 941 `return verdict is CHANGED` (so row 1 never calls `_propagate`, plan lines 895-897). Today's code preserves the version: Isabelle_Semantic_Embedding/semantic_interpretation.py:949-951 `if rec is None or rec.semantic_digest is None: version_to_write[i] = (rec.version if rec is not None and rec.version else epsilon)`. Parent CHECK_OUTDATE_PLAN.md:273 defines ε only for 首写 (first-written) entities, and I2 (CHECK_OUTDATE_PLAN.md:236) allows a version change only on a bump/mint. Counterexample (theory T, counter = 100): A is a constant whose record is {digest: None, version: 57, interpreted_at: 57, interpretation: present} — locally stale by parent §4.4, hence a seed. B is a constant with `B.deps = [uk(A)]` and record {digest matches the wire, deps: [uk(A)], version: 60, interpreted_at: 80}. At scan, `_contrib(A)` takes the wall branch (ver 57 > 0, ia 57 > 0, eff*(A)=57 <= 57) so eff*(B) = max(60, 57) = 60 <= 80: B is NOT a seed and starts `_NOT_ENROLLED` with a prefilled result. A's gate takes §3 row 1, writes version = w.counter_value() = 100, mints nothing, propagates nothing. After the run eff*(B) = max(60, contrib(A) = 100) = 100 > interpreted_at(B) = 80: B is stale, was never enrolled, and semantic_store.ML:2008-2013 marks T interpreted with the current (process id, serial), which semantics.py:869-878 then uses to skip T for the remaining life of this Isabelle process. The same shape hits every dependent of every legacy never-digested record in the theory.
findings.proposed_fix: Make row 1 preserve an existing version, exactly as the code it replaces does: `version, baseline = (rec.version if rec is not None and rec.version else w.counter_value()), text`. State the resulting invariant explicitly in §5.3.1/§14 — "within a run a tracked entity's version can only rise through `mint()`, and every `mint()` runs `_propagate`" — so the soundness argument is about a property the writer enforces rather than an assumption. (Residual, worth one sentence in §3: for a genuinely first-written entity ε is now read at write time, so it drifts upward as the run mints; a dependent that already carried the new entity's key in its stored deps can be left stale the same way. Reading ε once, at scan time, and carrying it on the task closes that too and costs no write, so it stays D14-compatible.)

findings.title: With the task holding every entry, an answer for a `_NOT_ENROLLED` entry starts a gate and can mint a version nothing authorised
findings.claim: §15.8 step 7 builds the `InterpretationTask` over ALL of the theory's entries so a non-seed can be enrolled later. That also puts every entry's label into `results`/`_label_to_idx`, which is the addressing table the `answer` tool checks — so the agent can now submit a translation for an entry the scan proved fresh and never showed it. §15.3's `on_answer` has no `_NOT_ENROLLED` arm: it falls through to `self.state[idx] = _GATING; self.start_gate(idx)`, so the volunteered text is gated, judged against the stored baseline, and on a CHANGED verdict MINTS a version and enrols that entity's dependents. Today this is structurally impossible: the task is built only over `uncached`, and an answer for any other entry is rejected as "Unknown entry".
findings.evidence: Plan lines 1053-1057 ("over ALL of the theory's entries (not today's `uncached` sub-list)"), plan lines 1057-1058 ("Non-seeds start `_NOT_ENROLLED` with `results` prefilled from the store"); plan lines 821-831 — the `on_answer` body branches only on `_DONE` and `_GATING`. Today: Isabelle_Semantic_Embedding/semantic_interpretation.py:1173-1179 builds the task with `entries=[entries[i] for i in uncached]`, and :592-593 `if key not in task.results: errors.append(f"Unknown entry: {key!r}")`. The invitation is in the tool description itself (:582 "You may also resubmit an entry to correct a previous answer") and in the end-of-batch message (:639 "If you noticed any mistakes in your earlier translations, correct them now") — with the full theory now addressable, "earlier translations" spans entries this run never sent. Consequence: a mint, and therefore a re-interpretation cascade, that no seed and no enrolment produced; it also breaks D7's "n is a LOWER BOUND on the live run's work counted from the seed set" in the one direction the dry run cannot bound, and §5.2's "an entity is interpreted at most once per run" reasoning silently acquires a second entry point.
findings.proposed_fix: Give `on_answer` an explicit `_NOT_ENROLLED` arm and make it non-minting: either reject it (return the entry to the tool's `errors` list, keeping today's "Unknown entry" semantics for anything the run did not ask for — the safest, since the agent was never shown the entry's statement), or treat it exactly like the `_DONE` correction of D11 (`Semantic_DB.update_interpretation`, text only, gate fields untouched). Whichever is chosen, state it in §5.3.1 beside the five states so that "only a seed or an enrolled entity is ever gated" is a property of the state machine rather than of what the agent happens to send.

findings.title: `_write`'s untracked branch dereferences `rec` when the entity has no stored record, crashing the gate of every new theorem-alike entity
findings.claim: `version = (rec.version or w.counter_value()) if e.deps else None` evaluates `rec.version` unconditionally when `e.deps` is non-empty. `rec` is `task.recs[idx]`, the record as stored before the run (plan line 881, and plan line 802 `self.recs = recs or [None] * len(entries)`), which is `None` for any entity not yet in the store. A newly added lemma/rule — a theorem-alike entry, `semantic_digest` None, `deps` non-empty, no record — therefore raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'version'` inside `gate_write`, which §5.4 turns into a `GateError`, which fails the task group and therefore `interpret_file`: the theory is not marked and the whole run dies. This is the commonest entry shape in any theory being interpreted for the first time.
findings.evidence: Plan line 923 `version = (rec.version or w.counter_value()) if e.deps else None`; plan line 881 `rec = task.recs[idx]  # record before this run`; plan line 802 `self.recs = recs or [None] * len(entries)`. The code being replaced guards for exactly this: Isabelle_Semantic_Embedding/semantic_interpretation.py:945-947 `if e.deps: version_to_write[i] = (rec.version if rec is not None and rec.version else epsilon)`. The tracked branches are safe (row 1 covers `rec is None`, and the UNCHANGED branch at plan line 931 is reached only when `rec is not None` per plan line 885), so the hazard is confined to this one line — which is why it is easy to miss in review and certain to fire in step 5's first live run.
findings.proposed_fix: Carry the existing guard over verbatim: `version = ((rec.version if rec is not None and rec.version else w.counter_value()) if e.deps else None)`. Better still, since three of the four branches need "the stored version, else ε", hoist it once at the top of `_write` (`stored_version = rec.version if rec is not None else None`) and let each branch read that, so no branch can reach a `None` record again.

findings.title: `_write` recomputes `ia` after the branch, so persistent-theory entries are written with `interpreted_at = 0` instead of None
findings.plan_sections: §15.5 `_write` (lines 918-948, esp. 924 vs 934); §3 table row "persistent theory" (line 98); D15; §6.3
findings.claim: The untracked branch sets `ia = eff_star(task, e) if e.deps else None` (line 924), but line 934 then executes `ia = eff_star(task, e)` unconditionally for every entry, discarding that `None`. For a persistent-theory entry (`semantic_digest` None, `deps` empty) `eff_star` reduces to `eff_value(version or 0, None)` = 0, so the record is written with `interpreted_at = 0` rather than None. That contradicts D15 and §3's last table row ("persistent theory | ... | None | None | None (all gate fields None)"), contradicts §6.3/parent §4.4's "字面 0 禁止作为存储值" (a literal 0 is forbidden as a stored version/interpreted_at), and breaks §10's own decision-table test ("the theorem-alike and persistent rows (no judge, today's fields)").
findings.evidence: Plan lines 923-925 (untracked branch, `ia ... else None`) versus plan line 934 `ia = eff_star(task, e)  # after this entity's own mint` — outside any conditional, inside the same `with` block. §3's row: plan line 98 `| persistent theory | no | answer arrives | None | None | None (all gate fields None) |`. The prohibition: Isabelle_Semantic_Embedding/semantics.py:550-552 (`counter_value` docstring: "a literal 0 is forbidden as a stored version/interpreted_at value"). Today's writer keeps it None: semantic_interpretation.py:390-398 `version, interpreted_at = (self.inv_fields[task_idx] if self.inv_fields is not None else (None, None))` with `tracked = version is not None`, and the scan never puts a persistent entry into `ia_snapshot` (:1130-1131 is guarded by `elif tracked`). The stored 0 is invisible to `_contrib` (which reads `r.interpreted_at or 0`, :1002), which is exactly why it will not surface as a failure — it will surface as a store whose persistent records no longer match the shape every other part of the plan asserts about them.
findings.proposed_fix: Compute `ia` in exactly one place, after the mint, and let it be None for the persistent case: `ia = eff_star(task, e) if (e.semantic_digest is not None or e.deps) else None`, deleting the assignment at line 924. Equivalently, restructure `_write` so each branch produces the complete 5-tuple (`digest, deps, version, ia, baseline`) and nothing is patched afterwards — then a branch that means "all gate fields None" cannot be partially overwritten by a later line.

findings.title: `tracked` denotes two different predicates inside §15.5; on the documented reading, theorem-alike records get a baseline and lose their stored version
findings.plan_sections: §15.5 `_gate` (line 884) and `_write` (lines 922, 932, and the parenthetical at 944-947); §3 table row "theorem-alike (WIP)" (line 97); D15; §0 glossary ("tracked entity")
findings.claim: `_gate` defines `tracked = e.semantic_digest is not None` (line 884). `_write` uses a variable of the same name at lines 922 and 932, and the parenthetical at lines 944-946 says it is `e.semantic_digest is not None or bool(e.deps)`. The two are not interchangeable: a theorem-alike entry has no digest but non-empty deps. Under the digest-only reading the snippet is consistent (theorem-alike takes the `if not tracked` branch and gets version = stored-else-ε, baseline None, digest None, deps from the wire — §3's row). Under the parenthetical's reading a theorem-alike entry is `tracked`, skips that branch, and falls into `elif verdict is None:` — because `_gate` never assigns a verdict for it — so it is written with `version = w.counter_value()` (its stored version discarded, another no-mint version raise) and `baseline_interpretation = text`, which §3, D15 and the Record field's own contract forbid for theorem-alike records.
findings.evidence: Plan line 884 `tracked = e.semantic_digest is not None`; plan line 922 `if not tracked:  # theorem-alike (deps present) or persistent` (needs the digest-only predicate to include theorem-alike); plan lines 944-946 "today's `tracked = version is not None` test (:392) becomes `e.semantic_digest is not None or bool(e.deps)` as the scan already uses (:1101)" (excludes theorem-alike from that branch). findings.title: `_EffStar` as written invites one memo shared between the scan and every gate, which a mint invalidates
findings.claim: §15.5 requires "the memo rebuilt per call" during the gate phase (correct: `rec_cache` mutates at every mint, so a memo that survives a mint is invalid) and in the same sentence prescribes "a small class `_EffStar(rec_cache)` so the scan and the gates share one implementation; the code inside is unchanged". The natural reading of a class constructed from `rec_cache` is one instance holding one memo, which §15.8 step 3 then reinforces by making the scan's evaluator `_EffStar(rec_cache)` over the same `rec_cache` object the task carries. The two requirements are only reconciled by remembering to construct a new `_EffStar` for every `eff_star(task, e)` call — precisely the "ask people to remember it" shape. The consequence is not a false-fresh (post-mint memo values are stale-low, and `_contrib` can only turn a lower `e` into `version(d)`, which is never above the true eff*), so it is conservative — but it produces silent, unbounded re-interpretation churn on every following run, and the analogous memo mistake is documented in this very file as a blocker.
findings.evidence: Plan lines 965-971. The invariant the memo depends on is stated in today's code as a property of the scan, not of a reusable object: semantic_interpretation.py:926-928 "Which digests changed is a fixed fact of this batch, so the eff memo built afterwards never goes stale", and the SCC-finalisation comment at :964-979 records the order-dependent false-fresh as "the 2026-07-28 review (R1, blocker)". Under the plan the premise "no record changes" holds during the scan and is FALSE during the gate phase (plan line 933 mutates `rec_cache` inside `_write`, plan line 960 inside `_propagate`).
findings.proposed_fix: Make the memo's lifetime equal to the snapshot it is valid for, by construction: give `_EffStar.__init__(rec_cache)` its own fresh memo and expose only `eff_value(version, deps)`, then have the scan build one instance and `eff_star(task, e)` build a new `_EffStar(task.rec_cache)` per call. Say so in one line in §15.5 ("one `_EffStar` = one snapshot of `rec_cache`; a mint ends that snapshot") instead of "the memo rebuilt per call", so the object cannot outlive its premise.

findings.title: The "prefilter skipped for the rest of the run" flag lives on the per-theory task, so each theory re-hits a dead embedding service and re-prints §12 #5
findings.claim: §5.4 and §12 #5 both scope the embedding failure to the run: "skipped ... for the rest of the run after a failed call", "Mid-run, embedding call failed (once per run)". §15.3 and §15.5 implement it as `task.prefilter_disabled`, an attribute of `InterpretationTask`, and there is one `InterpretationTask` per theory (§5.1: one theory = one `interpret_file` coroutine). Theories run concurrently as futures under `schedule_dag`, so a dead or unreachable embedding endpoint is retried once per theory and text §12 #5 is printed once per theory — up to the size of the cone. This does not damage the invalidation semantics (D2 makes the judge decide alone), but the user-visible text is approved as "once per run" and the retry storm is against a service already known to be down.
findings.evidence: Plan line 275 "and for the rest of the run after a failed call"; plan lines 646-647 "Mid-run, embedding call failed (once per run)"; plan line 806 `self.prefilter_disabled = emb_store is None` (an `InterpretationTask` field, plan lines 793-810); plan line 911 "print text §12 #5 once (`task.prefilter_disabled = True`)". One task per theory: plan lines 138-141 (§5.1) and semantic_store.ML:1986-1992/2008-2013, where `schedule_dag` forks one future per cone theory and each runs its own `interpret'`. The run-scoped object already exists and is already used for exactly this purpose: §15.8's "Ordering of the startup check's result" (plan lines 1066-1070) puts the resolved store on `connection.server.gate_emb_store`, and `server` is one object for the whole process.
findings.proposed_fix: Put the disable flag where the store already lives — beside `connection.server.gate_emb_store` (e.g. clear that attribute to None on the first failure) — and let `InterpretationTask.prefilter_disabled` read through to it rather than own it. Then "skipped for the rest of the run" and "printed once per run" are the same fact, and neither depends on how many theories the cone has.

accurate: The core of the invalidation design holds up under this lens. The enrolment rule of §5.3.1 is complete with respect to eff\*: within a theory, the only way a fresh (non-seed) entry can become stale during a run is a mint by one of its direct theory-internal dependencies, and every mint runs `_propagate` over exactly that set — so one-hop enrolment plus the wall property covers transitive chains correctly (if the intermediate B is judged UNCHANGED it is a wall and its dependents genuinely need nothing; if CHANGED it mints and propagates in turn; if it is still queued/sent/gating its own write computes `interpreted_at` after the mint is in `rec_cache`). The snapshot raise for a `_DONE` dependent is sound for the reason the plan gives — a `_DONE` entity's text was produced this run from the same source file and was itself gated against its own baseline — and, because `_write` and `_propagate` are synchronous with no `await` between them, the two orderings (j writes first / A propagates first) both land on a correct result, including for SCCs, where the SCC-wide `val` makes both members converge on the same raised value. Cross-theory propagation rests on `schedule_dag`'s ancestor-first futures (semantic_store.ML:1986-1992), which is real: a dependent always lives in a descendant theory, that theory scans after `interpret_file` has joined its gate group, and a minted version is strictly above every previously stored `interpreted_at`, so the dependent is a seed by the eff\* criterion. The seed set of §15.8 step 4 is the same set today's phases 1-3 compute, with the scan-time mint correctly removed and `rec.version or 0` correctly replacing `version_to_write`. Removing the scan's writes makes the dry run genuinely read-only and its "exact at zero" claim is right. The unified dep criterion keeps working end-to-end: a re-keyed target makes the dependent locally stale, it is re-interpreted, an UNCHANGED verdict still heals the stored `deps` (the gate write always carries the wire `deps`) without a spurious mint. The choice of a separate `baseline_interpretation` field over reusing `interpretation` (§6.2) is what stops "unchanged" drift from accumulating, and the field is correctly outside `_EMBEDDED_DOC_FIELDS`, so `update_gate_fields` needs no vector invalidation while `put_interpretation` does. The nested-transaction shape is also fine in practice: I checked that a read transaction opened inside an open write transaction on the same py-lmdb environment neither deadlocks nor sees the uncommitted put, which is what `eff_star`'s `_rec_of` does inside `gate_write`, and `rec_cache` covers the only key whose uncommitted state matters.
